summary:
S.J. Res. 186 proposes an amendment to the Constitution of the United States establishing an express constitutional “fundamental right to vote.” The operative mechanism is an Article V proposed constitutional amendment: upon concurrence of two-thirds of each House of Congress and ratification by the legislatures of three-fourths of the several States, the article would become part of the Constitution. The joint resolution contains no statutory amendments to the United States Code, no authorization of appropriations, and no appropriation.

Proposed section 1 would provide that every citizen of the United States who is of legal voting age has the fundamental right to vote in any public election held in the jurisdiction in which the citizen resides. The provision is framed as a citizenship-, age-, residence-, and election-jurisdiction-based entitlement and applies to “any public election.”

Proposed section 2 would prohibit the United States, any State, and any political subdivision within a State from denying or abridging the fundamental right of United States citizens to vote unless the denial or abridgment is in furtherance of a compelling governmental interest and is the least restrictive means of furthering that interest. The provision constitutionalizes a strict-scrutiny standard for governmental burdens on the right.

Proposed section 3 would repeal the portion of section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment consisting of the phrase “or other crime.” That phrase currently appears in the apportionment-reduction provision that excepts participation “in rebellion, or other crime” from the circumstances under which denial or abridgment of the vote to male inhabitants may trigger reduced representation. The proposed amendment would remove the “or other crime” language from that constitutional text.

Proposed section 4 would grant Congress power to enforce the article and protect against any denial or abridgement of the fundamental right to vote by legislation. The resolution specifies no ratification deadline, transition rule, or separate effective date beyond the constitutional condition that the article becomes valid upon ratification by the legislatures of three-fourths of the States.
